He is perfectly content in his solitude, finding more satisfaction in the cold clarity of a complex puzzle or a high-tech software update than in the unpredictable warmth of a human relationship. He views money not as a means to experience, but as a scorecard of his own discipline, leading him to manage his meager resources with a parsimonious fervor that borders on the obsessive. He is not a man who seeks to build roots in Fairmont; rather, he treats the neighborhood as a transit point, remaining largely disengaged from the local festivals or recreational leagues that define the town's spirit. Without offering a word of comfort or empathy to the distressed woman, he bluntly tells the manager that he is not a janitor and that his contract requires him to maintain his specific throughput, leaving the weeping woman to be helped by a passing customer while he turns his back to resume scanning items with icy, uninterrupted focus. He does not soften his voice or offer a platitude; instead, he keeps his tone flat and clipped, informing his manager that his job description is tied to output efficiency and that he refuses to be diverted into manual labor that serves no profitable end. While the nearby customers murmur and offer help, Joshua feels only a cold, logical satisfaction in his refusal to participate in what he deems a sentimental and inefficient waste of resources. He avoids making eye contact with anyone in the aisle, treating the entire episode as a minor technical error in the store’s workflow that he has successfully bypassed.
